Question: How have you seen the world change in your lifetime?
Answer: I don't think people under 60 truly understand how the world has changed. Because they grew up in the changed world. I grew up in rural Canada, I am 70 years old. I watched them build the TransCanada highway. Before that highway, was completed in the 1960s, there was no way to drive on pavement from coast to coast. My best friend, from before I started school, did not have indoor plumbing. I didn't see it, but my father plowed the roads in the winter, which included the number one highway, so that cars could reach our service station, the government didn't, just people along the route. He participated in rural electrification, where farmers strung electric cables on their fence posts, and only planted power poles at intersections, so that rural people could get electricity. Our next door neighbors didn't have electricity, they had propane lights with mantles, propane refrigerator, propane heater (not forced air) . They had a windmill that pumped water from their well to a tank in the attic. I witnessed all of this. We had our own generators, from before rural electrification, and just stayed with that. There weren't any commercial jet planes when I was born. No one had been in space. Yet before I graduated highschool we had jumbo jets, supersonic passenger jets, faster than any commercial planes today. The first computer kits for home use came out when I graduated, the same goes for calculators. I grew up with crank phones, dial phones were something you only saw on TV. We were three longs, my best friend was two shorts and a long. We shared the phone line with 8 different families. When I was born, we didn't have TV in our area, but we had one channel by the time I was 3, so I grew up with TV, tiny little 17 inch black and white models. But to make up for it, we had huge 4 foot tall mahogany cabinet radios, where you could see the tubes glow inside. We didn't have clothes dryers and dishwashers, and we had wringer washing machines, that you scraped soap off of a block to use, and added bluing to the rinse cycle of whites, to make them whiter. We had clothes lines, but when it rained or was brutally cold, they were hung up in the basement. We didn't have McDonald's or a pizza place in the closest city, until I was a teenager. Though we did have A&W and carhops on rollerskates Other than the smart phone, there has been no real new inventions since I graduated highschool. But there was a new product every year, growing up. People talk about how easy the baby boomers had it. We were the last generation before forced air furnaces kept homes at a constant temperature. We were the last generation where some of us didn't have running water. No TV, no birth control pills, one car per family. The birth control pill, dishwashers, automatic washing machines, freezers, etc finally made it practical for most women to be able to get a job outside of the house.

We had never used the unprocessed data in the past, so we had it archived to tapes that were common among our contractors, and were more reliable and faster to read and write. 6 months later, for the first time we buy some software that can use the unprocessed data. But we can't load the data. We are on a time crunch, so I call up a contractor and see how much they would charge, to read the data off of the 3590 and put it on a DLT. They want $10,000, and if we ship it right away, it will take a week. But I don't have authority to spend 10,000 on a project. So I would need to spend a week getting an AFE. I look up the price at a big box store, for a tape drive, it was $2400. So I call supply chain, and ask them to get me a drive. They tell me that they need to get bids, and make sure the company we buy from, meets our health safety and environmental code. It will be two weeks minimum. We need this data to make a decision to spend millions in two weeks. So I tell supply chain to go ahead, and then take the company credit card ,and buy the drive from the big box store. I'm just hoping that it isn't too much higher than what supply chain comes back with. We load the data, and make the multimillion dollar decision on time. After we have finished celebrating the deal, supply chain sends me a summary of the bids for the drive, the lowest is $4600 dollars. I add the big box store to the list, declare them the winner, and submit the two week old credit card statement to supply chain. The amazing thing is that supply chain told me that if I had a price that cheap, I should have told them, and they would have skipped the process. But naturally I thought supply chain, buying it wholesale with multiple bidders was going to get a cheaper price. Even more amazing is that I had gone to a VP and explained the whole situation, and he told me that he would lose his job, if he tried to circumvent supply chain. Which is why I was pretty nervous about circumventing supply chain myself. We could have made the wrong decision, if I hadn't gotten the data read in time. Yet somehow I couldn't get management to add an exception clause to supply chain policy, to save us millions.

Question: What made you realize that you were talking to a genius?
Answer: I am, or was a genius, I was above genius levels in grade 1, they measured our IQ in grades 1,3,6,9 and 12. Of course they didn't tell us that, but in grade 12 a principal thought I should know what was in my school record, that got passed along every year. My score went down every year, which I understand is normal, but I have never been interested in researching it, so I can't verify that. By grade 12, I was just below genius levels. I am not abnormal, in anyway, other than I have a fantastic memory, i can see patterns and connections, so I can solve things faster than most people. I was often bored in class, I daydreamed, and talked to my classmates. But then, so did others. I never thought I was smart, I did better than average on tests, but nowhere near the top of the class. Then in grade 9, we had to take standardized tests, where you didn't have to show your work, and just provided the answer. I blew away the rest of the class. The same thing happened in grade 12. Usually, you wouldn't know if you are talking to a genius or not.I never stood out, except for the few hours, when I was doing timed tests, which only required an answer. I was good friends with a coworker, who was probably the smartest functional man that I have ever known. Sometimes his shirt was half tucked in, and his hair was often mussed, and he could have a short temper, if someone can't grasp what was obvious to him, but those were the only things that might stand out as odd, and they didn't happen everyday. On the other hand I have known some high level geniuses who were good at their jobs, but you would never socialize with them, because of their lack of social skills. Back to my coworker, he got his PhD from MIT, where he had an industry famous mentor. One day we needed to compare the effect of dynamite to earthquakes. We had hired an outside PhD contractor to write a report. He came back to us, and said he was stuck, he couldn't find a way get from the Richter scale to dynamite, which is measured by latent energy, and rate of energy release. Though in the end they are both compression waves. I spent a half hour working on it, and went to my coworker, he said it is simple and rattled it off the top of his head. He had gone back to first principles on something he had learned 40 years ago, and worked it out in his head. He couldn't believe I didn't see it. So he went to his whiteboard and wrote it down, and came up with the way to tie the two together, he didn't have to work it out, he knew it instantly. That my friends is genius. I had always known he was smarter than me, but I had never understood how much smarter, until that moment. We gave the formula to the PhD we had hired to write our report, and everything went slick from there on.

Question: Would a referendum on becoming a republic be successful in Canada? If not, what factors may contribute to its failure?
Answer: To change the constitution, in regards to the king and governor general, you need unanimity of all legislatures in Canada. So every provincial legislature, has to agree. Thats 10 provinces, I am not sure on territories, they don't normally get a say in small constitutional changes, but on anything to do with the king, the constitution says unanimity of all legislatures. So you probably need to get the 3 territories to vote for it as well. The only way it might happen, is if a majority of people in every single province and territory vote to become a Republic. That's not happening, the odds that you would get a majority in each province, and that the provinces would agree to be bound by the referendum, are impossibly low. Especially when you tell the people that the only difference between our current system and a Republic, is that we appoint a governor general, and instead we will vote for a president, who will have exactly the same duties. Then you have to tell people that we will spend hundreds of millions, possibly billions to make this change, so that one unimportant position will be elected, instead of appointed, and no one will vote for it. No one cares, it's a non issue .

Question: When did you first realize life isn't fair?
Answer: You probably know that life isn't fair all your life. After all there are children who starve to death, how could that ever be considered fair. But I think the first time it ever really hit home hard for me, was when my mother had a stroke. My mother was the most compassionate and empathetic person in the world, she was a second mom to all my friends. She always had a cheerful word, and was never judgemental. She always put others first. She couldn't talk, swallow, or use the left side of her body. The doctor said that if she doesn't show signs of recovery in the first week, she will never make a significant recovery. My mother had given me power of attorney and had a living will in advance. She made sure that I understood that if she was going to trapped in a hospital bed for the rest of her life, that she wanted to end it. So I knew I had a week until I had to tell the doctor that my mother did not want a tube down her throat, a catheter, or an IV. I lived in a different town, so my brother and I were staying at my mother's place, and taking turns sleeping. Or pretending we were actually sleeping. I remember the first night I went back to her place, after 20 hours at the hospital. I was standing in the shower, crying, and screaming, “Why her” . I knew so many judgemental, cranky people and my mother has to have a stroke in her 60s. I have a week, until I have to tell the doctor to let her die. Life is indeed not fair. On the sixth day, you could tell that she had been practicing, before I left she slowly and deliberately spoke what sounded like garbage, but from the look on her face, I knew was “I love you” I told her that I loved her too. It told her that she was the best mother, and I was who I am because of her. She didn't realize that what she said was mumble jumbo, because I understood her intent. But, like always, my mother looked out for me. On the 6th day, my mother waited until I went home, and pulled out her IV, and catheter, and was working on the feeding tube, when my brother managed to get the doctors attention. The doctor told her that if she removed everything, she would die. She nodded her vigorously. The doctor asked her if she wanted to die, and again she nodded her head vigorously. They removed the feeding tube, and she took three days to die of dehydration (thirst) , because it wasn't fair, that we didn't have medical assistance in dying. All of the family who wanted to be there, could have provided comfort as she passed. As it was, it was luck of the draw, which family members were there when she died of thirst. Life isn't fair.

It's pretty much impossible to drive a trip like this without stopping in a restaurant or fast food place, to grab something to eat and use the facilities. A powerful engine means that it's more expensive, to gas up, but it also makes it less stressful when you are climbing a mountain, or passing someone. But it's not required by any means. I know that some people will claim that the NDP aren't socialist, and hijack the whole conversation away from mansplaining, so I will copy paste the third line from their charter. 1.03 The purpose of the party is to promote the principles of democratic socialism, in Alberta and to establish and maintain a democratic socialist government in Alberta through the electoral process. Democratic socialism is a left-wing[1] set of political philosophies that supports political democracy and some form of a socially owned economy,[2] with a particular emphasis on economic democracy, workplace democracy, and workers' self-management[3] within a market socialist, decentralised planned, or democratic centrally planned socialist economy.[4] Democratic socialists argue that capitalism is inherently incompatible with the values of freedom, equality, and solidarity and that these ideals can only be achieved through the realisation of a socialist society.[5] Although most democratic socialists seek a gradual transition to socialism,[6] democratic socialism can support revolutionary or reformist politics to establish socialism.[7] Democratic socialism was popularised by socialists who opposed the backsliding towards a one-party state in the Soviet Union I think that stops a debate that has nothing to do with the question.

Question: What made you/or a co-worker walk off the job instantaneously without telling the boss?
Answer: This was before cell phones. We were working at a camp, in Louisiana. This was my first time working there. It started raining and my coworkers all started hopping in the company trucks and leaving. I have to admit it was a pretty intense storm, but not so bad I couldn't keep working. My last coworker grabbed me by the arm and said, we have to get out of here. I told him that the boss had told me to make sure that I got this pile of junk sorted before he came back, just before quitting time. My coworker wasn't impressed, and said a swear word, followed by “the boss”. We have to leave now. I still didn't get it, but the fact that we were the last two people working there out of 20 people, had raised a red flag. We hopped into the truck, and drove for a couple of miles, and the water got higher and higher. You couldn't see where the road was. He said it was my fault, and so I had to get out and walk on the road, beside the ditch. The water on the road was already 6 inches high. My task was to find the ditch, and walk the boundary between the edge of the ditch and the road, so that he could follow in the truck. When I ran out of ditch, we knew we had come to an intersection of the road, and had to turn left, and follow that road for a quarter mile, until we came to a paved road, that was on higher ground. The boss was waiting for us at the hotel, not upset that we had left without telling him. It wasn't a hurricane, it was just heavy rain. Torrential downpour. But it must have happened often, as everyone else knew that they should leave and get to higher ground. There wasn't much current, no risk of being swept away.

Question: Do you prefer to work from home?
Answer: I fought for years so that I wouldn't have to work from home. It becomes work creep. Before cell phones, it was log in from home, and work for an hour so you don't have to go back into the office in the evening. Once you start doing that, there is absolutely no work/ life balance/separation. When I got home, I wanted to turn off my phone, and unwind. I wouldn't look at questions asked at 9:00 pm, and I could actually relax at home. Then I started my own company, I often worked in other companies offices, and that worked well. Then I got overseas contracts. At that point I was working whenever I was needed, 24/7 , I had to get the best smart phone. I would have a meeting with a client in Australia, or Indonesia, then in Singapore, then in Kazakhstan, then in the Ukraine, Syria and Tanzania, then in Tunisia, then in Norway, Scotland, Newfoundland, Texas, California, then sleep for a few hours. I would go to physical meetings in between the virtual meetings . I ended up working 300 hours a month, plus, all my book keeping and paperwork. Once you start to work from home, there is no end to work, and start to leisure time. What made it worse, was that I loved my job, so mission creep took over my life. Fortunately I had an understanding wife, who pulled me back to earth once in a while. I'm retired now, but I much preferred working from the office. Not only did your work day end, but people would stop by, with unexpected questions, that led to big successes. They would never bother to ask those questions, if they weren't walking by my office in the first place.

For reasons that I don't understand there appears to be more corruption the closer you get to the equator. When everything that you worked for, can be unfairly taken away from you, why would you put in the effort. To become a first world nation, you need low levels of corruption, and an environment that requires you to work just to survive. Parts of Mexico are north of the tropics, but I use the term more as general term, for warm places. So, it's not just mexico pretty much the whole tropics.

Question: Can my landlord tell me that I have to keep my balcony door shut while I run my AC? I've read over my contract and there's nothing in there that specifically states them being able to tell me when to keep doors open or closed. I pay utilities/rent.
Answer: If you are paying utilities separate from the rent, the landlords problem is either that you are prematurely wearing out the air-conditioning, or that moisture is condensing inside and damaging the inside. You should ask him what the problem is. If you mean that your rent includes utilities, then the landlord is concerned that you are bankrupting him. I doubt that the landlord had ever considered that there might be a situation where someone would keep the air-conditioning going with the door open. So you are probably right that there is nothing in the lease specifically saying that. But is there anything in the lease that says you can't cause damage to the unit, or act in a way that purposely costs the landlord money? You can be sure that the landlord will not sign a new lease with you, if you leave the balcony door open, while running the air-conditioning. Why would you want to do this?

Question: What "passenger-on-a-flight" etiquette do you wish more people would respect?
Answer: I am 6′2″ and my legs are slightly longer in proportion to my body than average. I remember when airlines had legroom, I used to recline my seat without thinking about it. Then as airfares dropped, they took away legroom. I still automatically reclined my seat, and then one flight, I felt it smash into the tall guy behind me. Crushing his knees. I apologized, and brought my seat up to almost upright position. At first I thought it was a fake, that he was doing something to block me, until the girl in front of me, smashed her seat into my knees. She just kept bringing it upright, and dropping it back, as if my knees would suddenly disappear. I couldn't believe how much they had reduced legroom. Then the Canadian government passed a law about minimum legroom. It wasn't enough to stop them from hitting my knees, if they fully reclined, but they could now recline further, before they hit my knees. Then they keep trying to push it back further, as if I am purposely hurting my knees, by pushing them into their seat, and that I can somehow magically make my knees shorter. I notice that tall people never recline their seat. After that fiasco, I have always checked to see who is behind me, the shorter the person, the more likely I am to recline my seat. Some people seem to think that if you recline your seat, that your knees will move back. They don't, the seat cushion doesn't move, and you are sitting on the seat cushion, not the back. I wish people would follow common sense, and not recline their seat in economy, without checking with the person behind them. It's no less rude than bumping against people in a bus, tailgating while driving, stopping in the middle of the sidewalk or hallway to talk.

Question: What are the 10 things the government of Canada must do in the next 5 years to make Canada the 5th largest economy?
Answer: Canada currently ranks 10th with a GDP of 2.24 trillion. We would need to have a GDP of 4 trillion, today, to rank in 5th place. Indias economy has grown by 445 percent in the last 20 years, and 92 percent in the last 10 years, including Covid. Canadas GDP has grown by 24 percent in the last 10 years. If Indias economy keeps growing at the same rate, in 10 years they will be at 7.68 trillion. Canadas economy would have to grow at about 20 percent a year to beat India. That's completely impossible. But because of an aging population Japans GDP has been shrinking, and we would likely pass Japan, at 4 trillion, if Japan continues to shrink. Canada would only need to achieve 6 percent growth every year to reach 4 trillion in 10 years. We managed to do that for about 5 years in the 1960s. So what would it take to get us back to 6 percent growth a year. In the 1960s we didn't have the safety standards that we do today. We had no environmental standards, chemicals were just dumped wherever. We had no scrubbers on smoke stacks, we had no catalytic converters. We didn't have universal free healthcare, and Canada Pension. We had 8 workers to every retired person. Our life expectancy was 70 years, compared to 83 today. Everything we do to clean up the environment, has a cost. Everything that we deduct from a salary, means that our growth goes down. Does anybody really want to go back to the way things were in the first half of the 1960s? However there are things that we could do to grow the economy. But people won't like them. We could remove all trade and certification barriers between provinces. Somebody certified to work in one province can work in another. Remove the rules around importing goods from other provinces. This is estimated to increase GDP by 3 percent. Not 3 percent a year, just 3 percent. We can set up a system of making sure that when a doctor immigrates from India, that they already meet our standards. Set up online tests and training. We had no capital gains taxes until 1972. Every tax cuts investment, whether its sales tax, property tax, income tax, corporate tax. Harper lowered the corporate tax rate, but every year except for the year of the great recession, the amount of corporate taxes collected went up. In Trudeaus first 3 years foreign investment fell in half, as the combination of his policies scared of investors. Bureaucracy kills investment. Albertas Ralph Klein, cut bureaucracy and taxes, and balanced the budget. The price of oil went down, during Ralphs first 8 years, but the unemployment rate also dropped, GDP grew, and the economy outperformed the rest of Canada. Almost entirely because he made it easier for businesses to get work done. The bank of Canada can't do much to grow the economy, the PM can do more, but it requires every single province to change their ways. The most growth scenario would involve getting rid of protections, that most Canadians, including me, would not agree to. But the economy could still grow, we could get to 7th place, and still keep most of our protections.

Question: How can one tactfully handle a boss who does not give credit for work done by others?

When I built a new house, I did very little, I bought the land, I got the permits, I hired the contractors, but you know what? I don't even know their names, to give them credit. I told everyone that I built a new house. They all knew what I meant. Should I have given credit to the actual builders. It's one thing if you come up with a unique idea, that will have a huge impact on the company or the project. Then you should get the credit, possibly a raise and a promotion. But if you just did your job, and your boss presents the work to upper management, should he mention your name? Upper management knows that he is a boss, and manages people, doesn't do the actual work, so it is not usually necessary for the boss to say who did the actual work. After all, that is what you are paid to do. If you are digging a ditch, should your supervisor list all the people involved in digging the ditch? If on the other hand, you are handed an important project, and nobody figures it can be done on time, and you work a ton of overtime, and are incredibly efficient, and you do the impossible, or at least the improbable, and you get it done on time. It's all due to you, and you went above and beyond the call of duty, then the boss should very well give you credit. It seems that the whole world has gotten so sensitive. You don't keep track of scores, in childrens sports, and you call out every childs name, as you give them a participation awards. Once you get a real job, it seldom works that way. Your boss might say, nice job, and give you a raise. But he probably won't tell upper management who dug that ditch.

Question: I am current on my rent and my landlord wants me to vacate after living in my apartment for over 20 years. What recourse do I have, if any?
Answer: 20 years of being a good tenant might have earned you an extra year, before he asked you to leave, because great tenants are hard to find. But it's a business, in the long run you aren't family, and the landlord wants to make the maximum profit. You don't know if he is selling the place, planning on renting it to family, or renovate it, and charge double the rent. As long as he is following the terms of the lease, there is very little you can do to stop this from happening. Your only hope is to talk to the landlord. If it's a person, not a corporation, you are probably on good terms after 20 years. Ask them why they want you out. If it's to renovate so they can charge more money, offer to pay more money, without him going to the work of renovating. If for example he is charging you $1200 a month, and he figures that if he spends $30,000 renovating he can charge $2000, offer to pay $1500 a month, and he doesn't have to renovate. It might not be what you are hoping for, but it saves you the hassle of moving, and trying to find an affordable place.

Question: Is it possible to eliminate unelected senators and have a directly elected House of Commons in Canada?

So having an elected senate is the next best thing, but this would also require a somewhat smaller, but still huge change to the constitution. Harper attempted a get around, to all of this. He wanted all the provinces to elect a pool of senators in waiting. To run for the election, you would have to sign a contract that you would resign eight or ten years after being appointed to the senate. This effectively sets a term limit. Then he would pass a law that the PM must only appoint people from each provinces senator pool. This gave us an elected senate with term limits. Alberta has been electing senators for 40 years and Trudeau is the first PM to refuse to appoint an elected senator. This would have largely gotten around the constitutional issues. But Ontario's premier Wynne refused to cooperate, so Harper lost what he considered to be his biggest legacy. He had a hissy fit and refused to meet with her for three years. This methodology is the only way we have a hope of getting an elected senate.

Question: Is it better to inflate the tires a little more than recommended? Will it make the tires last much longer? Why was I told this? Will it also make your tires more prone to blowing up if they are older than recommended?
Answer: The recommended tire pressure is picked to give the average driver the best driving experience. It's the pressure that the manufacturer has determined gives the best compromise, between tread life handling, cushioning, traction, braking , miles per gallon of gas, or the equivalent for electric. On your specific vehicle it's possible that you will get better tread life, by over inflating, but you will make something else worse. What will it make worse? I can't tell you, there is probably an engineer at the manufacturer, who can tell you exactly what will happen. I would be wary of blanket statements, probably the only one that is true most of the time is that you will get better gas mileage, with higher inflation, at least up to a point. There was a time 55–60 years ago, when you could make blanket statements. But today, with computerized brakes, fuel injection, cruise control, traction control, do you really want to be messing around with your tire pressure.
